newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S., EU to meet at WTO on Cuba dispute - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU to meet at WTO on Cuba dispute - diplomats.

text.p: U.S. and European Union officials are to meet at the World Trade Organisation on Monday to consider names for a dispute panel in their row over the U.S. Helms-Burton law on investment in Cuba, diplomats said.
But they indicated there was unlikely to be any agreement since the United States was arguing that the controversial legislation, dictated by national security, was outside the remit of a WTO panel.
They said they expected Washington would hold back on agreeing to any nominations for the three-member panel -- a list of which is prepared under the rules by the WTO Secretariat.

The 130-member WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) agreed on November 20 last year to an EU request, backed by many other countries in Asia and Latin America, to create a three-member panel on whether the U.S. measures violated open trading rules.

Since then Brussels had appeared to hold back -- apparently heeding warnings that the case could cause major damage to the WTO and the dispute settlement mechanism that is at the core of the two-year-old organisation.
There was no formal comment from EU, U.S. or WTO officials in Geneva where the organisation has its headquarters, on what is widely seen as a highly-sensitive issue.

However, in remarks quoted on Monday by the London Financial Times, EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said Brussels would be pushing immediately to get the panel working, and would seek the help of WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero.
Ruggiero told reporters at the World Economic Forum in Davos at the weekend that he hoped the dispute could be solved between the two powers without going through the full panel process.
"The objective of the dispute settlement system is to facilitate the solution of disputes, not to impose rulings on governments," he said.
WTO officials feel the case could feed opposition in the U.S. Congress to membership of the trade body, seen by many U.S. political figures as a threat to national sovereignty.
"This is extremely dangerous territory for the whole organisation," said one trade envoy in Geneva.

Under Article 21 of the WTO's underlying treaty, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, member countries are allowed to waive the rest of the accord if they see their national security at threat.

The Helms-Burton law, named after its Congressional sponsors, was signed by President Bill Clinton after Cuba shot down two small planes flown by Miami-based anti-communist exiles last January. It has also been fiercely criticised by Canada.

The law aims at restricting investment by other countries in Cuba by allowing U.S. citizens to sue foreign companies in U.S. courts if they "traffic" in property nationalised after the communist takeover in Havana in 1959.
Clinton has twice suspended application of this section of the law, saying recently Brussels had signalled it would work with Washington to improve the human rights situation in Cuba.

But in his remarks cited by the Financial Times, Brittan said he also wanted action by Washington on another section of the law which provides for refusal of U.S. visas to executives of companies seen as violating its provisions.
Some trade diplomats say a WTO panel would have to determine whether the U.S. was justified under Article 21 in pleading a national security exception.

But others say the United States seems correct in arguing that the article's phrasing means if a country deems its security is at stake no WTO panel, made up of trade and not political experts, could rule on this.
